items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Was there anything else in Jasmine besides Bessie Smith and Jelly Roll that was planned but didn't...

ctx.x: Yeah. Worked in Bakelite, and the hard rubber, and all that kind of junk. So... Anyway, I imagine Columbia had quite a few of the Bessies there. As late as 1939 or so. But... Oh, I was going to say, this opera collector told me, once at one period, they knew that you could go up to Bridgeport and buy any original master that you wanted to, the metal plate, for $5 was the price they'd sell. including their early opera. They had some early 1900 or 19... from 1900 to 1905 period opera on a silver label, I think it…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: The interviewee (William Russell) discusses Jelly Roll Morton extensively as a subject of his research and interviews with other musicians (Norwood Williams, Johnny Wiggs, Simeon), but never claims a direct personal interaction or professional collaboration with Jelly Roll Morton himself.

ctx.x: What kind of music do you think they were playing? Would it differ in any way from say what they were playing in the middle 20s?

I would doubt it myself just from the evidence of people's styles not changing that rapidly. I can't, we don't have any records of them. Actually the original Dixieland was the first to record. It might have been of course they always called it ragtime. A lot has been made like for instance in Brun's book on Nick LaRocca always made a big point of that. That they were the first ones to use the word jazz. But not, I'm not trying to say the colored people were first or anything of that kind in this particular case…

You were talking about... Yeah, a lot of the Negroes down here, they're all crazy about him. They all try to imitate him. And yet occasionally you run across some of the old timers that'll say, well, he plays novelty music. It's not really good jazz.
